hints: Look carefully at the graph and notice where the sloping blood pressure line is above the dashed water potential line, and where it falls below it.
Remember that fluid leaves when blood pressure pushes out harder than solute effects pull back, and fluid returns when the pull back is stronger. Which change would keep the push stronger for longer?
walkthrough:
**Read what the graph is telling us**

Think of this as a tug of war along the capillary. At the arterial end, blood pressure is high and above the dashed line, so it wins and pushes fluid out to form tissue fluid.

At the venous end, blood pressure has fallen below the dashed line, so the pull back wins and fluid is reabsorbed.

**Link water potential to plasma proteins**

The dashed line is the water potential effect of solutes, mainly large plasma proteins that stay in the blood. They lower the water potential of plasma, so water is attracted back into the blood by osmosis.

More plasma protein means a stronger pull back. Less protein means a weaker pull back.

**Decide what causes excess tissue fluid**

Excess tissue fluid (oedema) means too much fluid pushed out and too little pulled back in.

If blood pressure is increased, the sloping line stays higher for longer. More fluid is forced out at the arterial end and less is reabsorbed at the venous end, so fluid accumulates in the tissues.

options.A: More large plasma proteins would lower plasma water potential further and increase water reabsorption, which would reduce tissue fluid, not increase it.
options.B: Higher blood pressure pushes more fluid out at the arterial end and opposes reabsorption at the venous end, so excess tissue fluid builds up.
options.C: Fewer proteins in tissue fluid raises its water potential, so less water is drawn out of the plasma, which would reduce tissue fluid formation.
options.D: Lower blood pressure pushes less fluid out and allows more reabsorption, so tissue fluid would decrease, not accumulate.
